common_name: Little Goblin Red Winterberry Holly (Dwarf Compact Shade-Tolerant Winterberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil, and site a male winterberry pollinator such as Little Goblin Guy nearby to ensure fruit set.

directions: This dwarf winterberry selection stays noticeably more compact than the species, making it a practical choice for foundation plantings or smaller gardens where a full-size winterberry would outgrow the space. It needs a male winterberry cultivar blooming at the same time nearby, since this is a female plant and sets its heavy crop of extra-large red berries only after cross-pollination. Grow it in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil, as it tolerates boggy conditions far better than most shrubs and is often used along pond edges or in rain gardens. The persistent red fruit holds on bare winter branches well into the cold months, providing a reliable late-season food source for birds.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, acidic soil in partial shade, pairing with a male winterberry such as Jim Dandy for reliable fruit set.

directions: This old, naturally occurring color form of the native winterberry replaces the typical bright red fruit with a true glowing yellow, giving a distinctive winter display against bare gray stems. Like other winterberries it is dioecious, so this female selection needs a male pollinator blooming nearby to set its abundant fruit crop. It performs best in consistently moist, acidic, organically rich soil and tolerates periodic flooding, making it well suited to rain gardens and low wet spots at the woodland edge. Birds eat the yellow fruit somewhat later in winter than they take red-berried forms, often extending the display further into the season.

common_name: Allemans Red-Twig Dogwood (Compact Dark-Stemmed Redosier Dogwood)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring in moist to wet soil in partial shade to full sun; Allemans stays more tightly branched than the species and tolerates boggy, poorly drained sites.

directions: Allemans is a tighter, more compact selection of native redosier dogwood with dense branching and dark red winter stems that hold their color well in cold weather. Flat clusters of small white flowers in late spring give way to white to pale blue berries that are an important food source for songbirds through summer and fall. It tolerates consistently wet, even swampy soil better than most shrubs, making it useful for streambank stabilization, rain gardens, or low spots that stay damp. Cut a portion of the oldest stems to the ground every few years to keep a steady supply of vividly colored young wood for winter interest.

common_name: Argentea Variegated Pagoda Dogwood (Silver-Edged Native Understory Tree)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in rich, moist, acidic soil in light shade; Argentea is slower growing and smaller in stature than the straight species pagoda dogwood.

directions: This variegated selection of the native pagoda dogwood carries the species' distinctive horizontally tiered branching but adds leaves edged in white, giving a lighter, more luminous effect in a shaded understory planting. Flattened clusters of small creamy white flowers open in late spring and are followed by small blue-black berries that ripen in summer and disappear quickly once birds find them. It grows well under the high canopy of larger trees, where its tiered form and pale foliage show clearly against darker greens, and it is noticeably slower and more compact than the green-leaved species. Keep the soil consistently moist and rich in organic matter, since both dry spells and deep shade-grown stress make the variegation prone to scorch or reversion to plain green shoots, which should be pruned out when seen.
